newsitem.title: UK: UK house prices rise in three months to May-RICS.
newsitem.headline: UK house prices rise in three months to May-RICS.

text.p: UK house prices stayed on their upward path and rose again in the three months to the end of May despite interest rate rises and uncertainty over the budget, the Royal Institute of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) said in its latest housing market survey.
The recovery continued to be led by the South East of England, but East Anglia, the West Midlands and Wales also made a strong showing.
The average number of properties sold increased again in May, although volumes are still well below those seen in 1994 and less than half the peak levels of the late 1980s housing market boom.
"Overall the relatively small number of properties for sale continues to be the driving force behind house price inflation," the survey said.
"There were around 25 percent fewer properties for sale in the three months to the end of May than in the corresponding period last year."
The survey said there was some evidence of stock levels beginning to rise in the areas where shortages have been most acute, such as London.

This was partly due to the decision of many so-called 'slump landlords' -- owners who could not afford to sell at depressed prices in the recession and rented property out -- that the time is right to market their properties, the survey said.
RICS said it expected more properties to come onto the market after the July 2 budget, the approach of which is causing some potential sellers to wait and see.

"On the demand side, (any) sudden abolition of mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) in the budget would be likely to dent some buyers' enthusiasm, especially in Northern regions where average prices are lower. This would be bad for the market and we have urged the Chancellor to phase any removal of this relief over five years." said RICS spokesman Ian Perry.
"A rumoured plan to raise stamp duty would also damage the fragile recovery in many areas outside London and the South."
